strengths: Novel reformulation of genomic sequence modeling as OCR-style document understanding with genuine innovation in problem framing
Comprehensive experimental validation across three progressive benchmarks (canonical regulatory, population-level robustness, genome-wide prediction) demonstrating consistent improvements
Impressive parameter efficiency: competitive/superior performance with 409M parameters vs. 7B/1.8B models; 256K-parameter linear probes match much larger baselines
Technical soundness with rigorous experimental design including controlled 1D vs. 2D CNN comparison (Table S2) validating core design choices

Exceptional reproducibility: detailed implementation specifications (Appendices E-G), hyperparameter search spaces, data construction procedures, and comprehensive evaluation metrics across all six OCR tasks

Interpretability advantages demonstrated through Grad-CAM analysis showing region-aware, localized attributions aligned with biologically meaningful loci (splice sites), contrasting favorably with diffuse base-level attention in sequence models
Thoughtfully designed six-task suite with clear separation of transcription, localization, and reasoning capabilities; design principles explicitly motivated
Consistent improvements across datasets: +5.37% DNALONGBENCH, +8.49% cross-species generalization, best whole-genome phenotype prediction with 12.3min inference vs. hours for Evo-2
weaknesses: Text rendering justification incomplete: DNA lacks inherent visual properties like natural text; why monospace text specifically vs. other 2D representations not explained. Compression ratio claims conflate visual tokens with base-level tokens without clear information-density comparison

Comparison fairness concerns: Evo-2/LucaOne use frozen feature extractors + linear heads while OpticalDNA applies full parameter updates; expert baseline (Avsec et al., 2021) is 3+ years old; window-based pretraining (2048bp) differs from some baselines

Heterogeneous task performance undermines universality claims: T1-T3 excellent (97%+ exact match) but T4 shows only 13% text-EM with rapid degradation at longer spans (Table S26); T5 localization accuracy near 0 at IoU≥0.99 despite 57-60% query faithfulness; T6 chromosome classification only 6-10% accuracy

Limited statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple runs reported. Small benchmark sizes (RiceSubBench: 6000 windows; RiceWGPB: 102-130 samples) raise overfitting concerns without statistical validation

Scalability questions: image rendering overhead not fully analyzed; maximum 450k bases tested (226 pages) but whole-genome scale (3B+ bases requiring 1500+ pages) feasibility unclear; practical advantage over sequence models for typical 10-100k range tasks not established

Generalization limitations: evaluated only on HG38 and rice genomes; no cross-organism transfer or held-out chromosome evaluation; unclear how model performs on genomic regions/populations distinct from pretraining data
Modest overall improvements despite novelty: 5-17% relative gains, while consistent, don't demonstrate transformative advances. Gap between claimed novelty and magnitude of practical improvement

Task performance discrepancies indicate incomplete framework: very low performance on T4 (masked completion) and T5 (subsequence localization) suggests visual representation suboptimal for certain genomic operations, though acknowledged 'dominant bottlenecks' remain unresolved

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three benchmark suites with multiple evaluation metrics and detailed ablation studies
Practical efficiency improvements demonstrated (e.g., 12.3 min vs. hours on 400M-base genome inference)
Extensive supplementary material (36 pages) with reproducible details on hyperparameters, tasks, and datasets
Thoughtful design of six genomic tasks bridging OCR and genomic operations
Interpretability analysis (Grad-CAM) successfully localizing biologically meaningful regions like splice sites
weaknesses: Overclaimed fundamental motivation: rendering DNA as 2D documents is presented as addressing inherent limitations, but this conflates sparsity (a property of sequences) with computational inefficiency (an algorithmic issue) that visualization doesn't fundamentally resolve

Misleading efficiency claims: '20× fewer tokens' compares visual tokens after fixed preprocessing against raw k-mer tokenization—not apples-to-apples with hierarchical pooling or sparse attention alternatives

Modest empirical gains with unfair comparisons: only +1.8% improvement over JanusDNA on main benchmark (DNALONGBENCH), weak 1D CNN baseline (0.528 AUROC), and conflated parameter counts in comparisons

Weak absolute performance on key tasks undermines core claims: T5 (subsequence retrieval) achieves 0.057-0.060 text-EM at strict IoU, T4 (masked completion) only 0.13 text-EM, contradicting claims about alignment with genomic reasoning

No ablation on critical design choices: rendering parameters (font size, line spacing, resolution, nucleotides per page) are fixed without justification; Table 7 shows resolution changes yield minimal accuracy variation (0.849-0.852), questioning whether 2D representation matters
Incomplete analysis of when/why approach works: no investigation of which genomic contexts benefit from 2D vs 1D, error mode analysis, or comparison with simpler hierarchical/sparse alternatives
Multi-page fusion architecture appears lossy: single attention layer with mean pooling across 250+ pages may lose critical information
Rice experiments confound effects: pretraining on japonica then evaluating on subspecies mixes organism-specific benefits from representation-specific benefits

strengths: Novel reframing of genomic modeling as OCR-style document understanding, genuinely creative and first-of-its-kind approach
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse benchmarks (DNALONGBENCH, RiceSubBench, RiceWGPB) with rigorous protocols and multiple competitive baselines

Significant practical efficiency gains: ~20× fewer effective tokens, ~985× fewer activated parameters than large models, with demonstrable inference time improvements (12.3 min vs. hours for 400M-base genomes)
Thoughtful and well-motivated task design (T1-T6) with clear design principles that systematically cover core genomic operations (reading, grounding, retrieval, completion)
Excellent reproducibility with extensive appendices specifying hyperparameters, data construction procedures, prompt variants, metrics, and evaluation protocols at exemplary detail level

Strong interpretability insights: Grad-CAM analysis demonstrates region-level processing that mirrors human reading patterns and concentrates on biologically meaningful regions (e.g., splice sites), contrasting favorably with base-level attention in sequential models
weaknesses: Modest performance improvements on primary benchmark: +1.4% over JanusDNA with linear probe (0.852 vs 0.840) and +1.8% with MLP, representing incremental rather than transformative gains

Weak performance on critical pretraining tasks raises questions about learning efficacy: T5 (subsequence localization) achieves only 0.57-0.60 text-EM and near-zero localization accuracy (0.0055 Det-Acc@IoU≥0.99); T6 (chromosome classification) achieves only 0.062-0.104 accuracy

Limited mechanistic understanding of why visual representation helps: no direct measurement of information density in rendered form, no analysis of learned visual features, and unclear why 2D structure specifically aids long-range genomic understanding

Rendering hyperparameter choices (640×640 resolution, font size 14, line spacing 1.6) appear somewhat arbitrary and are underexplored; Table 7 only demonstrates robustness to resolution on one benchmark with minimal variation (0.849-0.852 AUROC)

Architectural constraints may limit performance: visual front-end completely frozen, decoder only fine-tuned with LoRA; no ablations show impact of these design choices, potentially capping achievable gains

Unclear transfer mechanism between pretraining tasks and downstream performance: OCR-style tasks (transcription, grounding, completion) have no obvious connection to eQTL prediction or phenotype prediction; no analysis identifies which pretraining tasks contribute most

Potential fairness concerns in baseline comparisons: different pretraining protocols and data for baselines vs. OpticalDNA; Evo-2/LucaOne tested as frozen models on rice benchmarks; Expert Model baseline is much smaller (~252M parameters)

Missing analysis of failure modes, when visual representation hurts performance, and scenarios where approach may not apply; no evaluation on truly long-context sequences (>450 kb) or truly out-of-distribution organisms

strengths: Genuine conceptual novelty: First application of OCR/document understanding paradigm to genomics with well-motivated connection between sparse genomic signals and region-aware visual processing

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three progressively challenging benchmarks with extensive ablations, contamination analysis showing <1% train-test overlap, and k-mer containment analysis ruling out memorization

Strong results on important tasks: eQTL prediction achieves 0.852 AUROC with 256K trainable parameters (985× fewer than baselines with comparable performance); cross-subspecies generalization shows 8.5-13.9% improvements
Exceptional presentation and reproducibility: 47-page comprehensive manuscript with detailed task specifications, hyperparameters, dataset statistics, and six well-designed OCR-inspired genomic tasks
Practical efficiency gains: ~20× fewer effective tokens, superior throughput vs strong baselines, reasonable memory usage, and cross-species transfer demonstrating transferability

Thoughtful treatment of limitations: Honest discussion of T5/T6 failures, extensive robustness analysis (rendering, resolution, k-mer contamination), token bottleneck analysis, and ethics considerations
weaknesses: Modest empirical gains over strong baselines: eQTL prediction shows only 1.8% improvement over JanusDNA MLP (0.852 vs 0.840); RiceWGPB shows 3.6% improvement over Evo-2 (2.95g vs 3.06g RMSE). Gains are real but often marginal

Confounded comparisons: Different visual encoder (SAM-Conv-CLIP-L) and decoder (DeepSeek-3B) not controlled in baselines; NT-v2-500M and GENERator-1.2B evaluated with frozen backbones + linear probes; Evo-2 chunked at 70kb unfairly

Critical failures on important genomic tasks: T5 (subsequence localization) achieves only 0.62-6.8% Det-Acc at IoU≥0.50, 0-1.3% at IoU≥0.99; T6 (chromosome classification) achieves only 6.2-10.4% accuracy—essential for motif discovery and genome-scale understanding

Visual representation inadequately preserves fine-grained information: Task T4 (masked completion) achieves only ~13% Text-EM, contradicting claims of 'high-fidelity compression'; span-based ablation shows rapid degradation with mask length

Limited true long-context modeling: Pretraining operates on fixed 2,048bp windows; 450kb evaluation uses per-page feature extraction + mean pooling rather than end-to-end sequential modeling; unclear if benefits come from spatial structure vs efficient aggregation

Insufficient analysis of performance drivers: Single ablation compares only against DeepSeek-OCR backbone; no systematic ablation of visual encoding vs decoder capacity vs prompt-based training; unclear what components drive improvements

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple genomic benchmarks (DNALONGBENCH, RiceSubBench, RiceWGPB) with strong and consistent empirical results
Thorough reproducibility analysis including contamination checks (<0.5% train-test overlap), extensive hyperparameter details, and robustness studies across rendering variations
Impressive cross-species transfer results showing human pretraining generalizes to rice despite large evolutionary distance
Honest acknowledgment of limitations and weak performance on certain auxiliary tasks (T4, T5, T6)
weaknesses: Questionable conceptual foundation: 2D rendering is presented as merely a 'computational interface' without principled justification for why it's superior to other sparsity mechanisms (local attention, sparse attention, hierarchical pooling). DNA has no intrinsic 2D structure, making the OCR analogy imperfect

Unfair baseline comparisons: 1D vs 2D models use different architectural families (Table S2), confounding representation with architecture. Parameter count claims ('985× fewer') are misleading given the frozen 3.4B backbone. Many baselines evaluated in suboptimal configurations with frozen backbones and linear probes

Limited technical novelty: The approach primarily applies pre-trained DeepSeek-OCR to genomics with domain-specific task formulation. The visual encoder, decoder, and multi-page fusion module are straightforward applications of existing components without significant methodological innovation

Unclear source of performance gains: Missing critical ablation showing whether improvements come from (a) the 2D rendering or (b) using a strong vision-language model. Auxiliary OCR tasks show poor performance (T4: 0.13-0.16 exact match; T5: 0.57 query faithfulness; T6: 0.062-0.104 accuracy) yet paper doesn't explain why these should improve downstream tasks

Rendering introduces brittleness: Fixed-window layouts significantly underperform continuous rendering (0.758-0.774 vs 0.813 AUROC), suggesting model relies on continuous rendering properties. This is a disadvantage vs sequence models which don't require these hyperparameters (font size, line spacing, canvas size)

Limited scope of evaluation: Benchmarks mostly limited to human and rice genomes; whole-genome phenotype prediction uses very small test sets (21-26 samples). No evaluation on other important genomic tasks. No comparison to other efficiency mechanisms (local attention, sparse attention, etc.)

Modest practical improvements: Fine-tuning throughput improvement over JanusDNA only ~2.4× (Table S36). Still requires freezing 3.4B model and 8×H100 GPUs for ~11 days of pretraining, limiting practical adoption

strengths: Novel problem reformulation treating DNA as visual documents with clear motivation addressing structure-aware reading and understanding-driven compression in sequential models
Exceptional experimental rigor with three progressive benchmarks, thorough contamination analysis (0.279% leakage), and K-mer containment analysis proving no memorization
Strong and consistent empirical results: 0.852 AUROC on eQTL with 30× fewer trainable parameters than JanusDNA, outperforming models with 985× more parameters
Outstanding reproducibility with complete task specifications, hyperparameter search spaces, detailed training schedules, and comprehensive ablations across 47-page appendix
Interpretability advantages with Grad-CAM visualizations showing region-level processing concentrated on biological signals, contrasting favorably with fine-grained sequential attention
Comprehensive robustness analysis across rendering variations (font, density, aspect ratio), resolution degradation, and representation consistency under perturbations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in components—visual encoder (SAM-Conv-CLIP-L), decoder (DeepSeek-3B), and fusion modules are existing; contribution is primarily problem reformulation

Mechanistic understanding of why 2D works better remains unclear—benefit could be from vision model inductive biases rather than inherent superiority of visual formulation; 'understanding-driven compression' claim lacks rigorous validation

Rendering introduces arbitrary design choices (font size 14, line spacing 1.6) with limited justification and adds computational overhead without clearly capturing biological structure (no strand information, 3D structure)
Scalability concerns inadequately addressed: inference on 400M base genome takes 12.3 minutes; no analysis of time scaling with sequence length; fixed 640×640 rendering limits density

Task design issues: T6 (chromosome classification) completely fails (0.062-0.104 accuracy) suggesting poor transfer; T5 (retrieval) shows poor localization (Both-Acc≈0.09 at IoU=0.99); unclear if these six tasks are optimal
Unfair baseline comparisons—Evo-2 and LucaOne evaluated with chunked sequences (70k, 1.28k bp) rather than full context; different pretraining corpora and objectives

Computational efficiency claims overstated—fine-tuning throughput (0.12 M bases/s) not significantly higher than Caduceus (0.52); GPU memory (5.81 GB) higher than some baselines; rendering overhead not fully quantified
Limited statistical rigor: no confidence intervals or significance tests; some improvements modest (0.852 vs 0.840); single runs reported without stability assessment across random seeds

Missing ablations on alternative pretraining objectives and comparisons with vision-based sequence approaches; stronger 1D baselines (BiGRU, Performer) relegated to appendices showing only modest gaps
